slots.practicalActivity: Run the sentence 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog, but foxes rarely jump in real life.' through a public tokenizer tool (e.g. platform.openai.com/tokenizer) and count how many tokens it produces; then sketch the transformer's attention step by circling which earlier words you'd expect the model to attend to when predicting the word after 'lazy'.
slots.deliverable: A short annotated note showing the token count from the tokenizer tool and your attention-circling sketch.

slots.practicalActivity: Call an embeddings endpoint (e.g. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small, or a free Hugging Face model) on four short sentences — two similar in meaning, two unrelated — and compute cosine similarity between every pair in a short Python script.
slots.deliverable: A Python script plus a 4x4 similarity table showing the similar pair scoring higher than the unrelated pairs.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real document (a long email thread or article) and use a tokenizer to calculate how much of an 8K, 128K, and 1M-token context window it would consume; then compare the stated context window and parameter class of a 'small/fast' model versus a 'large/frontier' model and note the capability trade-off.
slots.deliverable: A one-page table: your document's token count against each window size, plus a short note comparing the two models' trade-offs.

slots.practicalActivity: Ask a model a specific, obscure, or deliberately fake question (e.g. about a nonexistent historical event or a real person's non-existent book) and capture the hallucinated answer verbatim; then rewrite the prompt to explicitly allow 'I don't know' and see whether the hallucination stops.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side transcript: the original hallucinated answer versus the corrected response after the prompt rewrite.

slots.practicalActivity: Without looking back at the lessons, write a one-page reference sheet from memory covering: what a transformer attends to, how tokenization splits text, what embeddings represent, how next-token prediction works, what a context window limits, and why hallucination happens — then check it against the lesson guides and correct any gaps.
slots.deliverable: A completed one-page Chapter 1 reference sheet, with corrections marked in a different color.

slots.practicalActivity: Research the current flagship model from each of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Meta, and build a comparison table listing context window size, approximate price per million tokens, and one notable strength for each.
slots.deliverable: A four-row model-comparison table with sourced figures.

lessons.title: Choosing a Model for a Task

slots.practicalActivity: For three sample tasks — a customer-support classifier, a code-generation assistant, and an offline on-device summarizer — decide whether an open-source or closed model fits better, name a specific real model for each, and justify the choice against the open-vs-closed trade-offs covered in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A three-row decision memo: task, chosen model, one-paragraph justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Using real per-million-token pricing from two providers' published pricing pages, calculate the monthly cost of a workload of 500,000 requests averaging 300 input / 150 output tokens each on both models, then note each provider's stated deprecation or sunset policy for the exact model version you priced.
slots.deliverable: A cost calculation table for both models, plus one sentence per model on its deprecation timeline.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page 'model selection memo' for a hypothetical new product feature of your choosing, stating the model you'd pick, its cost/latency/quality trade-off, and its open-source-vs-closed rationale, as if presenting it to a product manager.
slots.deliverable: A one-page model selection memo.

slots.practicalActivity: Get an API key for Anthropic's Messages API (or OpenAI's Chat Completions API) and make your first real call asking 'What is 2+2?' with max_tokens set to 50; print and inspect the full raw JSON response, labeling the stop_reason and usage fields.
slots.deliverable: The exact request JSON you sent and the response JSON you received, with stop_reason and usage labeled.

slots.practicalActivity: Write three different system prompts (e.g. 'terse technical expert', 'patient beginner-friendly tutor', 'skeptical devil's advocate') for the same user question, and call the API with each to compare how the system prompt changes the assistant's tone and content.
slots.deliverable: The three system prompts plus the three resulting responses, with a one-line note on what changed each time.

slots.practicalActivity: Call the API on the same creative prompt (e.g. 'write a one-sentence story about a lighthouse') three times at temperature 0 and three times at temperature 1, and compare how much the outputs vary at each setting.
slots.deliverable: The six generated outputs labeled by temperature, with a one-sentence conclusion about the variance difference.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short Python script that calls the API with streaming enabled (e.g. the SDK's stream context manager) and prints each text fragment to the console as it arrives, instead of waiting for the full response.
slots.deliverable: A working Python script that visibly streams tokens to the console as they're generated.

slots.practicalActivity: Define a real tool (e.g. get_weather or convert_currency) with a name, description, and input_schema; send a request that should trigger it; parse the tool_use block the model returns; and send a tool_result back to get the model's final answer.
slots.deliverable: The full three-message round trip — your request, the model's tool_use block, your tool_result, and the final answer — saved as a transcript.

lessons.title: The LLM API Request Lifecycle, End to End

slots.practicalActivity: Request structured JSON output from the model matching a schema you define (e.g. {name, age, occupation}), parse it to confirm it's valid JSON, then diagram the full request lifecycle for that exact call — request sent, model processing, stop_reason returned, your parsing step.
slots.deliverable: The validated parsed JSON object plus a labeled lifecycle diagram for that call.

slots.practicalActivity: Build one small Python script that combines everything from this chapter into a single request flow: a system prompt, a non-default temperature, streaming output, and at least one tool definition passed in the same call.
slots.deliverable: A single runnable Python script that exercises system prompt, temperature, streaming, and tool calling together.

slots.practicalActivity: Add real error handling to your Chapter 3 scripts: catch and retry on a rate-limit error, log every call's token usage to a file, and simulate a dropped connection to confirm your retry logic recovers.
slots.deliverable: The updated script with retry/error handling, plus a usage log file showing at least five logged calls.

slots.practicalActivity: For three sample use cases — a brand-voice chatbot, a tool that extracts structured data from invoices, and a general-purpose coding assistant — decide prompt-engineering vs. fine-tuning for each and justify the decision in one paragraph.
slots.deliverable: A three-row decision table: use case, chosen approach, justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a valid five-line JSONL training file for a hypothetical support-ticket classification task, then write the minimal JSON request body to create a fine-tuning job referencing that uploaded file.
slots.deliverable: A five-line .jsonl training file plus the fine-tuning job creation request JSON.

slots.practicalActivity: Research LoRA's actual trainable-parameter reduction — find real numbers from a paper or provider blog post comparing full fine-tuning vs. LoRA on a specific model size — and summarize the mechanism and the real savings in your own words.
slots.deliverable: A half-page written summary citing the sourced real numbers.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a short evaluation rubric (3-5 criteria) for comparing a hypothetical fine-tuned model against its base model on your earlier use case, then estimate the real training cost using a provider's published per-token training price against your JSONL file's token count.
slots.deliverable: The evaluation rubric plus a worked training-cost estimate.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a one-page decision-tree worksheet (fine-tune vs. prompt-engineer vs. RAG) and run five different scenarios through it, writing the resulting decision for each.
slots.deliverable: A completed decision-tree worksheet with five scenario decisions.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate images from an image-generation tool or API using three different prompts for the same subject, varying style, composition, and level of detail specified, and compare how prompt specificity changed the output.
slots.deliverable: The three generated images side by side with their prompts and a one-paragraph comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Send a real image plus a text question (e.g. 'what's happening in this photo?' or 'read the text in this screenshot') to a vision-capable model via its image content-block API, and evaluate how accurate the answer is.
slots.deliverable: The image used, the question asked, the model's answer, and your written accuracy assessment.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a short audio clip through a speech-to-text API and check the transcript's accuracy against what was actually said, then write a one-page decision memo on whether a real product you're familiar with should add multimodal (voice/image) input or stay text-only, based on cost and user-need trade-offs.
slots.deliverable: The transcript accuracy check plus the one-page multimodal-vs-text-only decision memo.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a one-page comparison of the multimodal API options tested this chapter — image generation, vision, and audio — with real cost and latency notes for each.
slots.deliverable: A one-page multimodal API comparison sheet.

slots.practicalActivity: Scope your own capstone chat application: choose its persona/system prompt, decide whether it will stream and whether it will use tool calling, and write a one-paragraph spec describing exactly what it will do.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph capstone project spec.

lessons.title: Capstone: Building a Simple Chat Application

slots.practicalActivity: Build the conversation-loop skeleton in Python: an empty messages list, a while loop that reads user input and appends it to messages, with a placeholder for the real API call — before wiring in streaming.
slots.deliverable: A runnable skeleton script with the input loop and growing messages list (no live API call yet).

slots.practicalActivity: Wire the real streaming call into your skeleton, with your system prompt set outside the loop, and get your first end-to-end streamed reply printing to the console.
slots.deliverable: A working chat script that streams a real reply from the API on each turn.

slots.practicalActivity: Have a real multi-turn conversation with your running chat app and confirm it remembers something you said two turns earlier; then deliberately comment out the assistant-message append and observe the model 'forget' context, documenting both runs.
slots.deliverable: Two transcripts: one showing working memory across turns, one showing the forgetting failure once the append is removed.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend your chat app with one real Chapter 3 feature — a tools parameter for a function/tool call, or structured JSON output instead of free text — and confirm it works inside the running conversation loop.
slots.deliverable: The updated chat app script with the new feature working, plus a transcript demonstrating it in a live conversation.

slots.practicalActivity: Record a short screen demo (or write a detailed walkthrough) of your finished chat application in action, and write a portfolio summary explaining which lesson from the course each piece of the app came from.
slots.deliverable: A demo recording or written walkthrough, plus a portfolio summary paragraph.

slots.practicalActivity: Polish your capstone project's README, push the finished chat application to a public GitHub repository, and do a final self-review confirming you can explain every chapter's core concept — transformers, the API landscape, request/response shapes, fine-tuning, and multimodal models — without notes.
slots.deliverable: A public GitHub repository link with a complete README, and a completed six-chapter self-review checklist.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can call a production LLM API directly end to end — chat completions, streaming, tool calling, and structured output — and make an informed, cost-aware decision about model choice, fine-tuning, and multimodal capabilities for a real product feature.
